children.topic: What a tort is, and its aims
children.note: A tort is a wrong done to a person that lets them go to a civil court and ask for compensation. It protects your body, your property, your land and your good name.

children.topic: A civil wrong, not a crime
children.note: A crime is a wrong against society, prosecuted by the state, and can end in jail or a fine. A tort is a wrong against a person, who sues privately and usually asks for money.

manas.q: How does a tort differ from a crime?

children.note: In contract, you owe duties because you agreed to them. In tort, the law imposes duties on everyone, whether or not there is any agreement.

manas.q: How does a tort differ from a breach of contract?

children.note: The main aim is to put the injured person back, as far as money can, where they would have been if the wrong had not happened.

manas.q: What is the main aim of tort law?

children.note: Knowing they may have to pay makes people, businesses and transport owners take more care. This is called deterrence.
Tort law protects interests the community values: safety of the body, quiet use of land, freedom of movement and reputation.
The same event can lead to both a criminal charge and a tort claim. A reckless driver may be charged in a criminal court and also sued by the injured passenger.
The person who was harmed and sues is the claimant (in Kenya often called the plaintiff). The person sued is the defendant.
Most torts need fault: the defendant acted intentionally or carelessly. A few, called strict liability, make you pay even if you took care.
Negligence is the most common tort. The claimant must prove five things in order: a duty of care, a breach of that duty, causation, damage that is not too remote, and actual loss.
First ask: did the law expect this defendant to be careful towards this claimant? Without a duty, there is no negligence claim.
Take reasonable care not to harm people you can foresee being affected by what you do. This idea comes from Donoghue v Stevenson (1932).

manas.q: What is the 'neighbour principle'?

children.note: For new situations, English courts ask: was harm foreseeable, were the parties close enough (proximity), and is it fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty?

manas.q: What are the three Caparo questions for a duty of care?

children.note: Some duties are well established: drivers to other road users, doctors to patients, employers to workers, makers to consumers of their products.
The defendant breached the duty if they did not act as a reasonable person would have in the same situation.
The standard is objective: what would an ordinary careful person have done? A learner driver is judged like any competent driver.

manas.q: Is the standard of care in negligence objective or subjective?

children.note: Courts weigh how likely harm was, how serious it would be, the cost of precautions and the value of the activity. Bolton v Stone shows a very unlikely risk may be ignored.
A doctor, engineer or advocate is judged against a reasonably competent member of that profession, not against an ordinary layperson.

children.topic: Causation: did the breach cause it?
children.note: The claimant must link the breach to the harm. If the harm would have happened anyway, there is no liability.
Ask: but for the defendant's breach, would the harm have happened? If yes, the breach did not cause it. See Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital.

manas.q: What is the 'but for' test?

children.topic: A new act can break the chain
children.note: A free, unexpected act of a third person or of the claimant can break the link between the breach and later harm (a new intervening act).
Even if caused, the defendant only pays for the kind of harm a reasonable person could foresee. The Wagon Mound (No 1) set this rule.
The exact way or extent of the harm need not be foreseen, only its general type, such as physical injury or fire damage.

manas.q: What is the test for remoteness of damage after The Wagon Mound?

children.topic: Take your victim as you find them
children.note: If the kind of harm was foreseeable, the defendant pays the full loss even if the victim was unusually fragile. This is the 'thin skull' rule.

children.topic: Damage: there must be real loss
children.note: Negligence is not actionable without harm. Typical loss is injury, damage to property, and money lost because of them. Pure money loss on its own is recovered only in limited cases.

manas.q: Can you sue in negligence if no damage was caused?

children.note: Even when all elements are proved, the defendant can reduce or avoid liability with a defence.
The victim was partly to blame, for example by not wearing a seat belt. Damages are cut by the victim's share of fault rather than refused.

manas.q: What is the effect of contributory negligence today?

children.note: A person who fully knew of a risk and freely agreed to run it cannot sue for it. Courts apply this rarely; knowing of a risk is not the same as accepting it.

manas.q: What must a defendant show for volenti non fit injuria?

children.note: A person hurt while reasonably rescuing someone endangered by the defendant's carelessness is usually not treated as having accepted the risk.
A claimant whose harm flows from their own serious wrongdoing may be refused damages, for example one burglar suing another during a getaway.

manas.q: What does the illegality defence (ex turpi causa) do?

children.note: Beyond negligence, tort law covers unsafe premises, interference with land, direct interference with people and property, and harm to reputation.
Whoever controls premises owes people who come in a duty to keep them reasonably safe.
The person with control over the premises, such as an owner, tenant or shop manager. There can be more than one occupier.
Invited or permitted visitors must be kept reasonably safe for the purpose they came for, such as a customer in a duka.

manas.q: What duty does an occupier owe a lawful visitor?

children.note: Occupiers must expect children to be less careful than adults, so dangers that attract children call for extra steps.
A clear warning can be enough for an adult visitor. Trespassers are owed a lower duty, mainly not to be exposed to known serious dangers.
Nuisance protects the use and enjoyment of land and public rights. Rylands v Fletcher adds liability for dangerous things that escape.
An unreasonable interference with a neighbour's use or enjoyment of land, such as constant noise, smoke or smells from a nearby workshop.

manas.q: What is private nuisance?

children.note: An unreasonable interference with rights the public shares, such as blocking a road. A private person can sue only if they suffered special damage beyond the public.

children.topic: The rule in Rylands v Fletcher
children.note: If you bring something dangerous onto your land for your own purposes and it escapes and causes damage, you are liable even without carelessness.

manas.q: What is the rule in Rylands v Fletcher?

children.note: The rule applies only to an unusual (non-natural) use of land, and only if the thing actually escapes from your land. In England it is now treated as a kind of nuisance.
Trespass covers direct, intentional interference with a person, land or goods. It can be sued on without proof of harm (actionable per se).
Making someone fear that force is about to be used on them, such as raising a fist at a tout. No touching is needed.

manas.q: What is assault in tort?

children.note: Intentional, unwanted physical contact with another person, such as a slap or a shove off a matatu step.

manas.q: What is battery in tort?

children.note: Unlawfully restraining someone's freedom to move, even briefly, such as locking a customer in a shop without lawful reason.

manas.q: What is false imprisonment?

children.note: Entering or staying on someone's land without permission, or throwing things onto it, such as a neighbour fencing into your plot in Kiambu.
Directly and intentionally interfering with another person's goods, such as taking or damaging their motorbike without consent.
Consent, reasonable self-defence and lawful authority (such as a lawful arrest) can answer a trespass claim.
A false statement, communicated to someone else, that lowers a person in the eyes of right-thinking members of society.
Libel is defamation in lasting form, such as print, posts or broadcasts. Slander is passing form, such as spoken words or gestures.

manas.q: What is the difference between libel and slander?

children.note: The words were published to a third person, refer to the claimant, and carry a meaning that damages their reputation.
Truth (justification); honest opinion on a matter of public interest; absolute privilege, as for evidence in court or debate in Parliament; and qualified privilege, as for an honest job reference.

manas.q: Name four defences to defamation.

children.note: Kenya has a Defamation Act. The Constitution protects free expression (Article 33) but says it must respect others' rights and reputation, alongside dignity (Article 28) and privacy (Article 31).

children.topic: Who pays, and what courts give
children.note: Sometimes a person pays for another's wrong or without fault. Courts mainly give money damages or an order to stop, and claims must be brought in time.
An employer is liable for torts of employees done in the course of their work, even though the employer did nothing wrong itself.
Covers authorised acts and authorised jobs done in a wrong way, such as a driver speeding on the route.

manas.q: When is an employer vicariously liable for an employee's tort?

children.note: A small detour while on the job keeps the employer liable. A 'frolic of his own' unconnected to the job does not.
As a rule, a person who hires an independent contractor is not liable for the contractor's torts. Courts look at control and how the work is organised.
In some torts you pay even though you took care, such as under Rylands v Fletcher. The aim is to put the risk on whoever creates an unusual danger.
What the court can order once a tort is proved.
General damages cover pain, suffering and loss of amenity. Special damages cover exact money losses, such as hospital bills, and must be specifically proved.

manas.q: What is the difference between general and special damages?

children.note: The court orders the defendant to stop, or not to start, the wrongful act, for example to stop a nuisance or a trespass.
In nuisance, the victim may sometimes remove the cause themselves, such as cutting back overhanging branches, without breaching the peace.

Tort claims must be filed within a set time, or they are usually barred. In Kenya the Limitation of Actions Act sets the periods; for most tort claims it is short (commonly three years). Check the Act.

children.topic: 🇰🇪 Kenya: where tort law comes from
children.note: Kenyan tort law is mostly common law inherited from England, shaped by Kenyan statutes, the Constitution and Kenyan courts.
The Judicature Act tells Kenyan courts to apply the Constitution and written law first, then English common law and equity as received. English cases are persuasive, not binding.
The rights to dignity, privacy and freedom and security of the person sit alongside tort law. Article 29 protects against violence and detention without cause.
Law Reform Act (including blame-sharing), Occupiers' Liability Act, Defamation Act, Limitation of Actions Act, Traffic Act, and the Insurance (Motor Vehicle Third Party Risks) Act.
Kenyan statutes, not the English Acts, govern areas like occupiers' liability and defamation. Always check the Kenyan Act before relying on an English rule.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Classic English and Commonwealth cases that Kenyan courts still cite as persuasive.
A snail allegedly in a ginger beer bottle. The House of Lords held a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the final consumer.

manas.q: What did Donoghue v Stevenson decide?

children.note: Auditors owed no duty to a takeover bidder relying on company accounts. Set the three-step test for a duty of care.
A cricket ball hit out of the ground injured a passer-by. No breach, because the risk was so unlikely a reasonable person would not guard against it.
A hospital sent away a poisoned man without examining him. Breach, but no liability: he would have died anyway, so the 'but for' test failed.
Oil spilled in Sydney harbour later caught fire. The Privy Council held a defendant pays only for foreseeable kinds of damage.
A reservoir burst through old shafts and flooded a neighbour's mine. Liability without proof of fault for a dangerous escape.
A policeman hurt stopping a runaway horse recovered damages. Rescuers are not treated as volunteers who accepted the risk.
Use IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Work through each element in order and say which side has the stronger argument.
A matatu driver overtakes on a bend on Thika Road at speed and hits a lorry. Wanjiku, a passenger without her seat belt, breaks her leg. The matatu owner employs the driver.
Can Wanjiku recover damages, from whom, and will her own conduct reduce them?
Negligence needs duty, breach, causation, foreseeable damage and loss. Employers are vicariously liable. Contributory negligence reduces damages.
A driver plainly owes passengers a duty. Overtaking on a bend at speed falls below what a reasonable driver would do, so there is a breach.
But for the overtaking there would have been no crash. A broken leg is an obviously foreseeable kind of harm in a crash.
She can sue the driver and the owner, who is vicariously liable because the driver was on the job. Motor third party insurance usually pays.
No seat belt may be contributory negligence if a belt would have reduced her injury, cutting her damages by a percentage. Volenti will not apply to an ordinary passenger.
Wanjiku is likely to succeed against the driver and owner, with damages possibly reduced for not wearing a belt. State this as a likely outcome, not a certainty.
Small slips that cost marks in tort answers.
Always deal with all of duty, breach, causation, remoteness and damage, even briefly. Do not jump straight to defences.
Causation asks whether the breach caused the harm. Remoteness asks whether that kind of harm was foreseeable. Treat them separately.
Knowing of a risk is not consenting to it. Courts prefer contributory negligence, which reduces damages, over volenti, which defeats the claim.
Trespass is actionable per se. Do not say a land trespass claim fails because there was no harm.

children.topic: Citing English Acts as Kenyan law
children.note: English statutes on occupiers, contributory negligence or defamation are not Kenyan law. Use the Kenyan Act or the common law principle.
In accident problems, always ask who employs the wrongdoer. The employer usually has the means and insurance to pay.
